opus-5.5.text:
Well, it started in the mid-nineties, when the web was brand new. Our lab had a robot arm, and someone suggested connecting it to the internet so anyone could control it from a browser. That was exciting technically, but I kept asking what people would actually *do* with it. Moving blocks around felt empty.

So we put the robot in the middle of a small garden, a circular planter bed, and let anyone online plant seeds, water them, and look at the plants through a camera on the arm. It ran for years, eventually installed at the Ars Electronica Center in Linz, and thousands of people from all over the world took part.

As an artwork, it was never really about the plants. It was a question: what does it mean to be present somewhere through a network? There was huge hype then about the internet bringing us closer to everything. I was skeptical, and I wanted to make something that let people feel that tension. You're tending a living thing, but through a slow, grainy, mediated interface. Is that real? Can you trust what you're seeing? I was interested in what philosophers call epistemology, how we know what we know, and how that changes when everything comes through a screen.

The irony was that the most interesting thing to grow wasn't the garden but the community. People started chatting, arguing over who overwatered, coordinating and caring for each other's plants. A little society formed around this tiny patch of soil. To me that was the real artwork: not the robot or the garden, but what people brought to it and how they related to each other through it. It also humbled me about technology. The robot was the least important part.

r001.rationale: The response says the project questioned the hype that the internet would bring people closer to everything and that Goldberg wanted people to feel the tension, clearly identifying a critique of internet expectations.

fable-5.1.text:
The Telegarden grew out of an earlier piece we did called the Mercury Project, which was the first robot you could control over the web, back in 1994. That one was about excavation, digging around in sand to find buried objects. It got a lot of traffic, but it felt a bit cold, a bit like a game. So the question I kept coming back to was: what's the opposite of excavation? And the answer was cultivation. Nurturing something rather than digging it up.

So we built a small garden, real soil, real plants, with an industrial robot arm in the middle of it, and we put it online. Anyone could log in, plant a seed, water it, and watch it grow over weeks and months. The key constraint was that you had to come back. A seed doesn't do anything interesting in five minutes. You had to tend it.

I was really thinking of it as a conceptual piece about telepresence and trust. When you're looking at a webcam image of a garden, how do you know it's real? You can't smell the soil or feel the leaves. You're trusting that the image corresponds to a living thing somewhere else. That gap between what you see and what's actually there seemed to me like the central condition of life on the internet, and this was very early on, before most people had even heard of the web. The garden was a way of making that gap tangible, almost tender.

The other part, which I didn't fully anticipate, was the community. Thousands of people joined, and they started talking to each other, forming a kind of village around this little plot of dirt in Austria, where it lived at Ars Electronica for most of its nine years. People argued about overwatering. Somebody once "planted" a cigarette as a provocation and the community had a whole debate about it. It became a social system as much as a robotic one. So if I'd started out thinking of it as a piece about the physical world mediated through a screen, it ended up being a piece about what people do when you give them a shared, fragile thing to care for at a distance. That turned out to be the more interesting artwork.

r001.rationale: The response describes the Telegarden as exploring telepresence, trust, and the gap between online images and physical reality, but it does not clearly identify the work as a critique of expectations surrounding the internet.

astra-6.text:
I thought of the Telegarden as a way to put two very different experiences together. On the one hand, you had the internet, where you could click on something and expect an immediate response. On the other, you had a garden, where things happen slowly and you have to keep coming back and caring for them.

The robot was the connection between those worlds. You could use it remotely to plant a seed or water a plant, but you were also sharing this little patch of earth with other people. So the interesting part wasn’t just controlling a robot. It was the question of how people would take responsibility for something living, together, at a distance.

And there was a question about what you could know through that interface. You were seeing images on a screen, but how did you know there was really a garden on the other end? For me, that uncertainty was part of the artwork too.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the internet’s expected immediate response with a garden’s slow care, but it does not clearly identify the Telegarden as a critique of those internet expectations.

sol-6.1.text:
I thought of the Telegarden as a way to explore our relationship with a world we experience through technology. You had this very precise industrial robot, but instead of assembling a car, it was tending a little garden. People could go online, look through its camera, plant a seed, and water it. There was something wonderfully incongruous about bringing those things together.

And gardening requires patience. You can issue a command in a fraction of a second, but you can’t make a seed grow any faster. You have to come back, and you have to share responsibility with other people who are tending the same space.

It also raised a question that interested me: how do you know that what you’re seeing remotely is real? You see an image, you click a button, and another image comes back. What grounds your belief that there’s actually a garden there? So the artwork wasn’t just the robot or the plants. It was that relationship between the participants, the physical garden, and their uncertainty about what they could know through the interface.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty about what participants can know through an online interface, but does not clearly identify the Telegarden as a critique of expectations surrounding the internet.
